entities.summary:
Ibn ʿAbd Rabbih (Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Rabbih) was a renowned Arab poet and writer, born in unknown, who lived from approximately 880 to 940 CE in Baghdad, Iraq, and died in 940 CE. He is best known for his extensive collection of poetry and prose works, including the famous “Iqd al-Far’id (The Jewel of the Far’id), which showcases his mastery of Arabic literature and his profound understanding of Islamic philosophy. His works have had a lasting impact on Arabic literature and culture, influencing prominent writers and scholars of the Islamic Golden Age.

He was a central figure in the Islamic literary world, known for his prolific output, which included numerous poetry collections, as well as translations of classical Greek works. Ibn ʿAbd Rabbih's poetry is characterized by its lyricism, depth, and philosophical complexity, often exploring themes of love, spirituality, and the human condition. His legacy extends beyond the realm of literature, as his works have shaped Islamic thought and culture, reflecting the intellectual and artistic achievements of the Abbasid Caliphate.

Ibn ʿAbd Rabbih's significance lies in his role as a bridge between Arabic literature and Islamic philosophy, as well as his contributions to the development of Arabic poetry and prose. His works have been widely studied and admired throughout history, and continue to be celebrated for their beauty, insight, and intellectual depth.

He is widely known for his work on the history of the Arabs, particularly his book on the history of the Umayyad caliphate. His writing played a significant role in shaping the Arab identity and preserving the cultural heritage of the Islamic world. Ibn ʿAbd Rabbih's works were highly regarded by his contemporaries and have been studied by scholars for centuries. He is considered one of the most important Arab writers of the medieval period, and his legacy continues to be celebrated in the Arab world.
